title: Medieval World Maps and Their Edges
description: Mappae mundi, the earthly Paradise, Gog and Magog, the monstrous races and two holy Atlantic islands

concepts.title: T-O Maps and the Hereford Mappa Mundi
concepts.contentHtml:
Learned medieval Europeans generally knew the earth was a sphere. They still drew world maps, called mappae mundi, that nobody steered by. Those maps arranged the inhabited world as history and theology as much as geography.

The simplest form is the T-O map, a diagram associated with Isidore of Seville's Etymologies (early seventh century). A ring of Ocean (the O) encloses three continents divided by a T of water, with the Mediterranean as the stem and the Don and the Nile as the crossbar. Asia fills the top half, Europe the lower left and Africa the lower right, and many versions assign them to Noah's sons Shem, Japheth and Ham. East sits at the top. An Augsburg printing of the Etymologies in 1472 included a T-O diagram, often cited as the first printed map in Europe.

The Hereford Mappa Mundi, made about 1300 and still kept at Hereford Cathedral, is the largest medieval map to survive, a single sheet of calfskin about 158 by 133 cm. An inscription credits "Richard of Haldingham and Lafford" with making it. Jerusalem sits at the center, and Christ presides over the Last Judgment at the top. The circle holds about 420 towns along with biblical scenes, animals, plants and peoples.1 It cites the late Roman historian Orosius and draws on Alexander legends, bestiaries and older maps.

The map works as an encyclopedia of time laid over space. You could trace a path from the Garden of Eden at the top, through the events of the Bible, to the ends of the earth. At the edges, texts rather than travelers supplied the details, and much of what's there never existed.

concepts.title: Paradise, Gog and Magog, and the Monstrous Races
concepts.contentHtml:
On the Hereford map, the earthly Paradise is a round island ringed by a wall of fire. Like everything at the edges of a mappa mundi, it had a textual pedigree: Genesis places Eden "eastward" with four rivers flowing out of it. With east at the top, Paradise usually sat at the summit of the map. Many medieval writers believed Eden still existed in the far east, cut off from human reach. Columbus took this seriously. In 1498, meeting the huge freshwater outflow of the Orinoco, he wrote that the earthly Paradise might lie inland.

Gog and Magog fused biblical prophecy (Ezekiel 38 to 39, Revelation 20) with the Alexander Romance, in which Alexander shuts savage nations behind a gate of bronze or iron. In the Quran (sura 18), Dhu al-Qarnayn builds a barrier against Yajuj and Majuj, and the ninth-century geographer Ibn Khurradadhbih records an envoy sent by the caliph al-Wathiq to find it. Mapmakers drew the enclosed peoples in northern Asia, waiting to break out at the end of time. In the 1240s Matthew Paris linked them to the invading Mongols.

The monstrous races came mainly from Pliny the Elder's Natural History (77 CE), which drew on earlier Greek writers about India, and from the third-century compiler Solinus. On the Hereford map many of them crowd the far southern edge of Africa: Blemmyae with faces in their chests, one-legged Sciapods, dog-headed Cynocephali. Augustine had argued that such beings, if they existed and were rational and mortal, descended from Adam.

concepts.title: Antillia and Saint Brendan's Isle
concepts.contentHtml:
Two of the Atlantic islands on late medieval charts came from religious legend. Saint Brendan's Isle grew from the Navigatio Sancti Brendani Abbatis, a Latin tale probably written in the ninth or early tenth century about the Irish abbot Brendan of Clonfert (died c. 577). In it, Brendan and his monks sail for seven years among strange islands, celebrate Easter on the back of a whale, and finally reach the "Promised Land of the Saints". It's a religious romance.

Even so, the island went onto maps. The Hereford map labels a group of islands off Africa "the six Fortunate Isles are the islands of Saint Brendan". In the Canaries it became San Borondón, an island people on La Palma and El Hierro reported seeing on the horizon. Spanish searches from the sixteenth century to 1721 found nothing, and cloud banks and atmospheric effects are the usual explanations.

Antillia, the Island of Seven Cities, rests on an Iberian legend. Around 714, as Muslim armies conquered the peninsula, an archbishop of Porto and six bishops sailed west with their people, founded seven cities on an island and burned their ships. Antillia first appears clearly on a 1424 portolan chart by the Venetian Zuane Pizzigano, as a large rectangle far west of Portugal. Martin Behaim's 1492 globe tells the legend (dating it 734), and Paolo Toscanelli's letter of 1474 treated Antillia as a stepping stone toward Asia, an argument Columbus knew.

After Columbus, Antillia faded from most maps, but its name survived in the Antilles of the Caribbean. The seven cities moved on too, reappearing in New Spain as the Seven Cities of Cíbola (Lesson 5).

title: Prester John: The King Beyond Islam
description: A rumor of 1145, a forged letter of about 1165, and a legend that steered Portugal toward Ethiopia

concepts.title: A Priest-King in the East (1145)
concepts.contentHtml:
The first datable mention of Prester John comes from Otto, bishop of Freising, in his chronicle. Otto records that in 1145, at the papal court at Viterbo, he met Hugh, bishop of Jabala in Syria, who had come west after the fall of the crusader city of Edessa in 1144. Hugh spoke of a certain John, "king and priest", a Nestorian Christian ruling beyond Persia and Armenia, who had defeated the Persian kings and marched to help Jerusalem, only to be stopped at the Tigris, which he could not cross.

Historians usually connect the story to a real battle. In 1141, at Qatwan near Samarkand, the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar was crushed by Yelü Dashi, founder of the Qara Khitai empire in Central Asia. Yelü Dashi was not a Christian (the Qara Khitai rulers were mostly Buddhist), but a great defeat of a Muslim ruler far to the east, passed along by rumor, could easily become a Christian victory. Christians of the Church of the East, the "Nestorians", really did live across Central Asia, which made the idea plausible.

The timing mattered. Edessa had fallen and the Second Crusade (1147 to 1149) was being preached; Latin Christians wanted to believe the Muslim world was encircled. "Prester" is simply a shortened form of "presbyter", priest. From the start, then, Prester John was a figure of hope: a Christian ally somewhere beyond the enemy, whose location shifted with whatever Europeans knew, or thought they knew, about the far side of the Islamic world.

concepts.title: The Forged Letter and the Mongol Hope
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1165 a letter began circulating in Latin Europe, supposedly sent by "Presbyter Johannes" to the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos. It describes a realm across the "three Indias" where 72 kings pay tribute and the apostle Thomas lies buried, where a river of precious stones flows and a fountain restores youth. Amazons, monstrous races, a jeweled palace and a mirror in which the king can watch his whole empire complete the picture. The text was copied, expanded and translated into many vernacular languages over the next three centuries.

The letter is a forgery. Its author is unknown, but its Latin and its borrowings from Western sources (Alexander legends, stories of Saint Thomas in India) point to a European cleric, and textual study of its versions has suggested an Italian or southern French origin. Its purpose is still debated: utopian fantasy, satire, crusade propaganda or a learned game. It was taken seriously all the same. In 1177 Pope Alexander III wrote to a "Magister Johannes" and sent the reply east with his physician, Philip, who was never heard from again.

When the Mongols struck Persia, crusaders at Damietta in 1221 heard of a "King David", a descendant of Prester John, destroying Muslim armies; the conqueror was in fact Genghis Khan. Friars such as John of Plano Carpini (1245) and William of Rubruck (1253) went east partly in hope of Christian allies. Marco Polo later identified Prester John with Toghrul, ruler of the largely Christian Keraites, whom Genghis defeated. Each new piece of knowledge about Asia pushed the kingdom somewhere further off.

concepts.title: Ethiopia and the Portuguese
concepts.contentHtml:
From around 1300 Europeans increasingly placed Prester John in Africa. Ethiopia fitted the profile: an ancient Christian kingdom, its church linked to Alexandria, separated from Europe by Muslim states. Medieval "India" was elastic enough to include East Africa, so the move did not feel like a contradiction. Ethiopian envoys reached Europe in 1306, and the Dominican Jordanus, writing about 1330, described the Ethiopian ruler as the one Europeans called Prester John. Ethiopian monarchs never used the title, and envoys at the Council of Florence in 1441 were puzzled to hear it.

For Portugal the legend became strategy. Gomes Eanes de Zurara, chronicler of Prince Henry "the Navigator", listed among Henry's motives the wish to find a Christian prince in those lands who would help against the Moors. In 1487 King João II sent Pêro da Covilhã and Afonso de Paiva overland through Egypt to scout the Indian Ocean and seek Prester John. Paiva died on the journey; Covilhã reached Ethiopia around 1493 and was never allowed to leave.

A Portuguese embassy finally arrived in 1520 and stayed six years. Its chaplain, Francisco Álvares, published his account in 1540 as True Information about the Lands of Prester John of the Indies, the first detailed European eyewitness description of Ethiopia. The alliance became military in 1541, when about 400 Portuguese musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama landed to help Emperor Gelawdewos against Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi of the Adal sultanate. Gama was captured and killed in 1542; Ahmad died at the battle of Wayna Daga in 1543.

title: Islands That Never Were
description: Hy-Brasil, Frisland, Sandy Island and Bermeja, and the reasons charts kept them

concepts.title: Hy-Brasil: A Circle West of Ireland
concepts.contentHtml:
Unlike Plato's Atlantis, which exists only as a story in two of his dialogues, the islands in this lesson were drawn on working charts. The most durable is Brasil, often written Hy-Brasil, placed in the Atlantic west of Ireland. It appears on a portolan chart by Angelino Dulcert in 1325 (as "Bracile") and then on chart after chart, often as a neat circle split by a channel. The origin of the name is debated, with Irish roots most often proposed. The country Brazil was named later, after brazilwood, a red dye timber.

People went looking. In 1480 a Bristol ship sailed west to search for "the island of Brasylle" and was driven back by storms after about nine weeks, and a Bristol venture of 1481 seems to have had the same goal. Irish folklore held that the island was usually hidden in mist and showed itself once every seven years.

The island lasted so long because charts were copied from earlier charts, and a mapmaker who dropped a traditional island risked leaving out something real. Fog banks, low cloud and mirages could look like land to sailors who expected land. Over time the island shrank into a "Brazil Rock", which some British charts still showed in the mid-nineteenth century before hydrographers removed it. Nobody could prove the island was absent, and it stayed on charts for more than five centuries.

concepts.title: Frisland and the Zeno Map (1558)
concepts.contentHtml:
Some phantom islands were honest mistakes; Frisland was very probably a fabrication. In 1558 the Venetian Nicolò Zeno the Younger published letters and a map he said he had found among his family's papers. They described voyages in the 1380s and 1390s by his ancestors Nicolò and Antonio Zeno, who were shipwrecked on a large northern island called Frisland, served its prince Zichmni, and heard of lands further west named Estotiland, Drogeo and Icaria.

The leading cartographers of the age, including Mercator and Ortelius, copied the map, and Frisland sat between Iceland and Britain on European maps for about a century. It misled real navigators. In 1576 Martin Frobisher, sailing to find the Northwest Passage with maps derived from Zeno, sighted the coast of southern Greenland and took it for Frisland, and on his 1578 voyage he went ashore and claimed "Frisland" for Elizabeth I.

Most historians now judge the story a hoax, or at best a heavy reworking pieced together from earlier maps and travel books. Frederick W. Lucas's study of 1898 showed how much of the map was borrowed, and Venetian records place the elder Nicolò on trial for embezzlement in Venice in 1394, when the letters have him in the north. Frisland itself may be a garbled image of the Faroes or Iceland. The modern claim that Zichmni was Henry Sinclair, earl of Orkney, and that he reached North America is speculation with no independent support. Frisland faded from most maps during the seventeenth century.

concepts.title: Sandy Island, Bermeja and the Copying Machine
concepts.contentHtml:
Phantom islands did not end with the age of sail. Sandy Island appeared in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, about 25 km long. The whaler Velocity reported "Sandy Islets" there in 1876, and British charts of the 1890s showed them. French hydrographers removed the island in 1974 and the Australian service in 1985, but it survived in digital coastline datasets and from there in Google Earth and scientific maps. In November 2012 the Australian research vessel Southern Surveyor crossed the spot and found open ocean about 1,400 m deep. The 1876 sighting may have been a raft of floating pumice; its digital afterlife was a copying error.

Bermeja ("reddish") was described off the north coast of the Yucatán Peninsula by the Spanish cosmographer Alonso de Santa Cruz in 1539, and it stayed on charts for centuries. In 2008 it suddenly mattered: an island there would have strengthened Mexico's claim to oil-bearing seabed in the "doughnut holes" of the central Gulf, areas beyond both Mexico's and the United States' 200-nautical-mile zones. A 2009 survey by Mexico's national university (UNAM), commissioned by the Chamber of Deputies, found nothing at or below the surface. Some Mexican legislators suggested the United States had destroyed it; the likeliest explanation is an early positional error that later mapmakers copied.

Three mechanisms recur across this lesson: copying, misperception (fog, cloud, pumice, mirage) and deliberate invention.

title: Mapped but Missing
description: The Mountains of Kong, Terra Australis, the Northwest Passage and Lake Parime

concepts.title: The Mountains of Kong (1798 to 1888)
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of the nineteenth century, maps of Africa showed a long east to west mountain range across the interior of West Africa, north of the Guinea coast: the Mountains of Kong. It began with the Scottish explorer Mungo Park, who in 1796, on his journey to the Niger, noted "some very distant mountains" to the south and was told they lay in a country called Kong. In 1798 the geographer James Rennell, the leading armchair authority on African geography, drew a long range on the map accompanying Park's Travels (published 1799).

The range did theoretical work. Rennell held that the Niger flowed east and ended in an inland basin where it evaporated, and a mountain barrier to the south helped explain why it never reached the Gulf of Guinea. Later mapmakers, from Aaron Arrowsmith in 1802 onward, copied and enlarged it, and some linked it to the Mountains of the Moon, the ancient supposed source of the Nile. Richard and John Lander showed in 1830 that the Niger does reach the sea, removing the range's original purpose, yet the mountains stayed.

The French officer Louis-Gustave Binger reached the town of Kong (in today's Côte d'Ivoire), a real Dyula trading center, in early 1888 and found no great range. After his account was published in the early 1890s, mapmakers began dropping the mountains, though a few atlases kept them into the twentieth century. The geographers Thomas Bassett and Philip Porter, who traced the range through dozens of maps, argued that it survived on authority: each map followed "the best authorities", and the best authorities had copied each other.

concepts.title: Terra Australis Incognita
concepts.contentHtml:
The belief in a great southern land is often traced to Greek arguments from symmetry: land in the north seemed to need a counterweight in the south. Ptolemy's Geography (second century CE) showed an unknown land closing off the southern Indian Ocean. Renaissance world maps by Mercator (1569) and Ortelius (1570) drew a vast Terra Australis wrapping the bottom of the globe, labeled as not yet known. Each new coast sighted in the southern seas, from Tierra del Fuego to New Zealand, could be read as a cape of the continent.

In the eighteenth century the Scottish geographer Alexander Dalrymple championed the continent as a populous land that could transform British trade. The Admiralty sent James Cook to observe the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, with sealed additional orders to search the South Pacific for it. On that first voyage (1768 to 1771) Cook charted New Zealand as two islands, not part of any continent, and mapped the east coast of Australia.

His second voyage (1772 to 1775) settled the question. With the Resolution and Adventure, Cook made the first recorded crossing of the Antarctic Circle on 17 January 1773 and reached 71°10' south in January 1774 before pack ice stopped him. He circled the globe in high southern latitudes and concluded that any southern land must lie within the ice, cold and of no use for settlement or trade. He was right. Antarctica, first sighted in 1820, is a real continent, but nothing like the temperate, populous land of the maps.

concepts.title: Passages and Lakes That Ought to Exist
concepts.contentHtml:
Wishful geography was not limited to land. For three centuries Europeans hoped for a Northwest Passage, a sea route north of America to Asia, and some sixteenth-century maps showed a "Strait of Anián" running through to the Pacific. Martin Frobisher (1576 to 1578), Henry Hudson (1610 to 1611, cast adrift by his mutinous crew) and William Baffin (1616) all probed the Arctic. Cook's third voyage searched from the Pacific side and was turned back by ice north of the Bering Strait in 1778. A passage did exist, but as a maze of ice-choked channels: John Franklin's expedition of 1845 vanished there with all 129 men, and Roald Amundsen made the first transit by ship only in 1903 to 1906.

Lake Parime was the South American version. Walter Raleigh wrote in 1596 that the golden city of Manoa stood on a great salt lake in Guiana, and Jodocus Hondius's map of 1598 drew an enormous Lake Parime with Manoa on its shore. Copied for two centuries, the lake faded only slowly. Alexander von Humboldt, after traveling the Orinoco in 1800, traced it to small lakes such as Amucu on the Rupununi savanna, and others pointed to the savanna's seasonal floods, which can turn grassland into a temporary sheet of water. Robert Schomburgk visited Lake Amucu in 1840 and found nothing like the lake of the maps.

title: Cities of Gold
description: El Dorado from a Muisca ritual to Raleigh's Orinoco, and Coronado's search for Cíbola

concepts.title: Guatavita and the Gilded Man
concepts.contentHtml:
El Dorado began as a man, not a place: el dorado means "the gilded one". The story belongs to the Muisca, goldworking chiefdoms of the plateau around modern Bogotá. Its fullest version comes from Juan Rodríguez Freyle's chronicle El Carnero, written around 1636, a century after the conquest, using what a nephew of the last lord of Guatavita had told him. When a new ruler took office, Freyle says, he was stripped, coated with sticky earth and covered in gold dust, then taken on a raft of reeds to the middle of Lake Guatavita, where he and his companions threw gold and emeralds into the water. Spanish writers mention a gilded chief from about 1541; the ritual fits Muisca offering customs, but the detailed account is late and secondhand.

The lake became a target. In the late sixteenth century the Bogotá merchant Antonio de Sepúlveda cut a deep notch in the crater rim, lowering the water until the cut collapsed, and recovered some gold and emeralds. In the early twentieth century a British company, Contractors Ltd, drained the lake through a tunnel, but the exposed mud set hard and little was found. Colombia placed the lake under legal protection in 1965.

In 1969 farmers found a small gold raft (19.5 cm long) in a cave near Pasca, carrying a large central figure and attendants, cast by the lost-wax method in gold, silver and copper. Charcoal left from its casting mold has been radiocarbon dated to about 1295 to 1410 CE. Now in Bogotá's Museo del Oro, it is often linked to Guatavita, but it was not found there and may depict another ceremony.

concepts.title: From Gilded Man to Golden City
concepts.contentHtml:
Spanish conquistadors reached the Muisca in 1537. Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada had left Santa Marta on the Caribbean coast in 1536 with several hundred men, most of whom died on the way up the Magdalena River. On the plateau the Spaniards seized gold and emeralds, and Quesada founded Santa Fe de Bogotá in 1538. In 1539 two rival expeditions, under Sebastián de Belalcázar from Quito and the German Nikolaus Federmann from Venezuela, arrived on the same plateau. The Muisca obtained much of their gold by trade rather than mining it, so the plunder was finite.

Once the Muisca were conquered, El Dorado detached from them and became a golden kingdom in the unexplored lowlands to the east. Gonzalo Pizarro left Quito in 1541 in search of it and of cinnamon forests; his lieutenant Francisco de Orellana, sent ahead for food, was carried down the Napo and the whole Amazon to the Atlantic. Antonio de Berrío led three expeditions toward the Orinoco between 1584 and 1590.

In 1595 Walter Raleigh captured Berrío on Trinidad and took boats up the Orinoco until rising floods forced him back. His Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Bewtiful Empyre of Guiana (1596) placed the golden city of Manoa on a great lake and repeated reports of the Ewaipanoma, a people with eyes in their shoulders and mouths in their chests, the Blemmyae of the medieval maps reborn. His last voyage, which sailed in 1617, ended with his men attacking the Spanish settlement of San Thomé, the death of his son, and his own execution in 1618.

concepts.title: The Seven Cities of Cíbola
concepts.contentHtml:
North of Mexico the gold legend took the form of seven cities. The Iberian tale of seven bishops founding seven cities on Antillia (Lesson 1) gave Spaniards a ready template, and new reports seemed to confirm it. In 1536 four survivors of the wrecked Narváez expedition to Florida reached Mexico City after eight years crossing the Gulf Coast and the borderlands: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Andrés Dorantes, Alonso del Castillo and Esteban (often called Estevanico), an enslaved Moroccan. They brought hearsay of large towns to the north.

In 1539 Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza sent the Franciscan Fray Marcos de Niza north with Esteban as guide. Esteban went ahead and was killed at the Zuni town of Hawikuh. Marcos reported that he then saw Cíbola from a distance, a city "more extensive than Mexico", and that it was the smallest of seven. Whether he came anywhere near it is still debated; some historians think his timetable makes the trip impossible.

The report launched the expedition of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado (1540 to 1542), with a few hundred Spaniards and well over a thousand Indigenous allies from central Mexico. In July 1540 they stormed Hawikuh and found a multistory adobe pueblo with stores of maize and some turquoise, but no gold. Coronado wrote to the viceroy that the friar had not told the truth in anything he said. Following new stories from a Plains captive the Spaniards called "the Turk", he marched in 1541 to Quivira, in present-day Kansas, and found villages of grass houses. The Turk was executed.

title: Ultima Thule and Hollow Earths
description: Pytheas's Thule, Halley's nested shells, Symmes's polar holes and the later lives of a name

concepts.title: Pytheas and Thule
concepts.contentHtml:
Some time around 330 to 320 BCE the Greek Pytheas of Massalia (modern Marseille) sailed out of the Mediterranean, around Britain and into the northern seas, and wrote a book, On the Ocean. It is lost. What survives comes from later authors who quote or summarize it, often with hostility: Polybius and Strabo treated him as a liar, while the geographer Eratosthenes and the astronomer Hipparchus used his observations of latitude.

According to these fragments, Thule lay six days' sail north of Britain, a day's sail from the frozen sea. Pytheas described a region where land, sea and air were not separate but blended into something like a "sea lung", a jellyfish-like mass that could be neither walked on nor sailed through; modern readers often take this for slush ice or freezing fog. Strabo also reports, without making clear that it refers to Thule, that people near the frozen zone lived on millet and wild plants and threshed their grain indoors for lack of sunshine.

The main candidates for Thule are Iceland, the coast of Norway, Shetland and the Faroes. Iceland fits the frozen sea and the long summer day, but it had no inhabitants until the early Middle Ages, which clashes with any reading that Pytheas met people there. Norway fits the farmers and the sailing time. The Estonian writer Lennart Meri proposed the island of Saaremaa in 1976, an idea few scholars accept. The surviving text cannot settle the question. Roman writers turned the name into a symbol: Virgil's phrase ultima Thule, "farthest Thule", in the Georgics made it the proverbial edge of the world.

concepts.title: Halley's Nested Shells and Symmes's Holes
concepts.contentHtml:
The hollow earth began as a serious scientific hypothesis. Compass needles do not point to true north, and by the late seventeenth century it was clear that this deviation, called magnetic variation, slowly changes from year to year. In 1692 Edmond Halley offered an explanation in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions. The earth, he proposed, is an outer shell about 500 miles thick enclosing two inner concentric shells and a central core. Each carries its own magnetic poles, and because they rotate at slightly different speeds, the combined field drifts.

Halley was also answering Newton's Principia, whose estimate made the Moon denser than the Earth; a partly hollow Earth eased that problem. In 1716 he added that glowing gas escaping from the interior might cause the aurora. He then gathered data at sea, commanding the Paramour on Atlantic voyages from 1698 to 1700 and publishing a chart of magnetic variation in 1701. The measurements were valuable; the nested shells were wrong. Modern geophysics traces the field's drift to flowing liquid iron in the outer core.

In 1818 John Cleves Symmes Jr., a former US Army officer living in St. Louis, mailed a circular declaring the earth "hollow, and habitable within", built of concentric spheres open at both poles, and pledged his life in support of the claim. He sought backers for an expedition to sail into the polar opening and lectured for years, widely mocked. His follower Jeremiah N. Reynolds turned the campaign into lobbying for a national voyage of discovery, which historians count among the influences behind the United States Exploring Expedition (1838 to 1842).

concepts.title: The Afterlives of Thule
concepts.contentHtml:
Thule never stopped moving. Tacitus says a Roman fleet sailing around Britain in the 80s CE glimpsed Thule in the distance, probably Shetland. In 825 the Irish monk Dicuil applied the name to an island where Irish clerics had stayed around 795 and the summer sun barely set, almost certainly Iceland. The Byzantine historian Procopius used it for part of Scandinavia. In 1910 the Danish explorer Knud Rasmussen founded a trading station in northwest Greenland called Thule, a name later used for a US air base and by archaeologists for the Thule culture, ancestors of the Inuit.

The name was also taken up by the far right. The Thule Society, founded in Munich in 1918 around Rudolf von Sebottendorf as a cover for a lodge of the Germanenorden, was a völkisch group: nationalist, racially antisemitic and attached to the idea of a lost northern homeland. A member, Karl Harrer, co-founded the German Workers' Party in January 1919 with Anton Drexler; Hitler joined it that September, and in 1920 it became the Nazi party. Rudolf Hess was a member, but there is no evidence Hitler ever attended, and the society had dissolved by about 1925. Postwar occult writers turned it into the hidden engine of Nazism, a myth historians such as Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke have taken apart.

The association still matters. On 1 January 2019 NASA's New Horizons probe flew past a Kuiper Belt object the team had nicknamed Ultima Thule. The nickname drew criticism for its Nazi-era associations, and in November 2019 the object was formally named Arrokoth, a Powhatan word for "sky".
